client: I've been having a really hard time at work lately, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything. There's this colleague of mine, Jessica, who keeps presenting my ideas in meetings like they're her own, and my manager doesn't seem to notice or care. It's making me feel like I'm invisible there, and I keep worrying that if she keeps this up, I'm the one who end up looking replaceable.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling invisible and anxious about your position — having your contributions go unrecognized is genuinely frustrating and hurtful, and those feelings are valid. I also notice you came here even while doubting it would help, which tells me a part of you is still looking for a way through this. I'd love to explore that with you — when you imagine the worst-case scenario of looking "replaceable," what does that situation actually look like to you?

client: Honestly, the worst case looks like me sitting at my desk one day and getting called into a meeting where they just... let me go. Like, no warning, no explanation, just "we've decided to go in a different direction," and I realize that nobody even noticed enough about what I do to fight for me to stay. That image really scares me because it confirms this feeling I already have that I'm just kind of background noise at work, easily swapped out for someone else.
therapist: That image is so vivid and painful, and it sounds like it carries a deeper fear — not just of losing a job, but of being fundamentally unseen and unvalued by the people around you. I want to gently ask you to look at that fear alongside the evidence: are there moments, even small ones, where your work *has* been noticed or appreciated at this job? I'm curious what comes up when you really sit with that question.

client: I mean... yeah, my manager did say something positive about a report I put together last month. But honestly, my first instinct is to dismiss it — like, she was probably just being polite, or she says that to everyone. It's hard to let those moments actually land as real when this underlying feeling that I'm invisible just keeps pulling me back under.
therapist: That instinct to dismiss the positive feedback is really worth noticing — it's a classic example of our minds filtering out evidence that doesn't fit the story we already believe about ourselves, and it's something we can gently work with. The fact that you *can* identify that moment, even while your mind is rushing to explain it away, is actually meaningful. What do you think it would feel like, even just for a moment, to let that compliment be real and true — to sit with it rather than dismiss it?

client: Honestly, just thinking about that makes me feel kind of uncomfortable, like there's this resistance that kicks in almost immediately. If I let myself believe the compliment was real, I think part of me worries that I'm being naive or setting myself up to be wrong about myself in some embarrassing way. It's easier to just brush it off than to sit with something that feels so uncertain.
therapist: That resistance you're describing is so understandable — if you never let the good things in, you can't be "wrong" about them, and in a way it feels like self-protection. But I wonder if that same protective wall that keeps out the uncertainty is also the thing that reinforces this feeling of invisibility, because it quietly filters out all the evidence that contradicts it. What do you think that younger, more protected part of you was originally trying to keep you safe from?

client: I think that part of me was trying to keep me safe from getting my hopes up and then being let down again. Like, if I expect nothing, I can't be devastated when nothing comes. But hearing you say it out loud like that... I don't know, it's a little uncomfortable because it makes it sound like I'm the one doing this to myself, and I'm not sure I'm ready to sit with that idea yet.
therapist: That discomfort you're feeling right now is actually a really important moment — it means something is shifting, and I want to honor how hard it is to even consider that idea without it feeling like self-blame, because protecting yourself from disappointment was a genuinely intelligent response to real pain you've experienced. Noticing the pattern isn't about fault; it's about gently asking whether a strategy that once kept you safe might now be costing you something. What do you think it might feel like to carry a little less of that armor, even in just one small area of your life?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe it's not about fault... but then there's this other part that immediately thinks, "if I let the armor down even a little, I'm just setting myself up to get hurt again." Like, the loneliness I feel now is painful, but at least it's a pain I know how to survive. I guess I'm scared that if I try to let someone in and it goes wrong, I won't be able to handle that kind of hurt on top of everything else I'm already carrying.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage to articulate — you've identified something really profound, that you've chosen a familiar pain over an uncertain one, and that makes complete sense when you're already feeling so stretched thin. I want to gently offer that the fact you *can* survive the loneliness actually tells us something important about your resilience — you're stronger than the part of you that fears being broken. I'm wondering, has there ever been a time in your life when you did let someone in and it turned out to be worth the risk?

client: I mean... yeah, there was one time, back in college. My roommate and I started out pretty awkward and distant, but at some point I just kind of broke down about some family stuff and she actually stayed up with me the whole night talking. It was good, it really was, but I guess part of me also remembers that we eventually drifted apart after graduation and that still stings a little, so I'm not sure it proves what you're hoping it proves.
therapist: That memory is so tender — it holds both things at once, the real comfort and connection you experienced *and* the grief of losing it, and I don't want to minimize either of those truths. But I'd gently point out that your mind went straight to the ending, when what you actually described first was a moment where you let someone in and they *showed up for you* — that happened, it was real, and it mattered. What do you think it says about you that even after that friendship faded, you still carried the warmth of that night with you?

client: I guess it says that I'm not completely closed off, even if it feels that way most of the time. But I don't know, Luna, part of me wonders if holding onto that warmth is actually making things harder, like I'm just reminding myself of something I can't get back. It's almost easier to focus on the ending because then I don't have to feel how much I miss having that kind of closeness.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that focusing on the loss is actually a way of protecting yourself from feeling the full weight of how much you *want* that closeness, because longing for something feels more vulnerable than grieving it. And the fact that you still miss it so deeply tells me that part of you hasn't given up on connection, even if another part is working very hard to convince you otherwise. I'm curious — if that part of you that still longs for closeness could speak freely, what do you think it would ask for?

client: That's... a hard question to sit with, because I think that part of me would just want someone to actually show up — not out of obligation, but because they genuinely want to be around me. But even saying that out loud makes me feel kind of pathetic, like I'm asking for too much or something I should have outgrown by now. I don't know if longing for that kind of closeness is realistic anymore, or if I've just been alone long enough that I've convinced myself it's safer this way.
therapist: What you just described — wanting someone to show up for you simply because they want to — is one of the most fundamentally human needs there is, and there is nothing pathetic or immature about it; in fact, it took real vulnerability to say it out loud. I want to gently challenge the idea that you should have "outgrown" this, because that belief itself sounds like another piece of armor, a way of shaming yourself out of needing what every person genuinely needs. Where do you think you learned that wanting this kind of closeness was something to be embarrassed about?

client: I think I learned it from my dad, honestly. He wasn't a bad person, but he was always kind of... distant, and whenever I'd want to spend time with him or get upset that he wasn't around, he'd say something like "you're too sensitive" or "you need to learn to be independent." So I just started telling myself the same thing, I guess, like I internalized his voice. It's weird to even say that out loud because part of me still feels like I'm making excuses or blaming him for something that's just... my problem.
therapist: What you just shared is genuinely important, and it's not about blame — it's about understanding where a belief was born, because a young child who was told their need for closeness was "too much" had no choice but to adapt by turning that critical voice inward and making it their own. The fact that you can now recognize that voice as something you *learned* rather than an absolute truth about who you are is actually a profound and meaningful shift. I'm wondering — if you could speak to that younger version of you who was just trying to get their dad's attention, what would you want them to know?
